{"self_assessment": "Impact: Our table built a large fish, with a rounded body, a left-facing nose and a swooping tail, and by the end nearly every standing domino was connected to the start, so one push could carry the whole outline. I contributed to that by making sure what stood on the table actually fell, not just what looked right. I found and fixed the jam just before the nose that had left the nose stretch disconnected, and I closed the stray domino in the belly seam.

Execution: I spent most of the ten minutes inspecting the run closely and repeatedly, checking where the fall would stop and why. That let me locate the specific breaks at the nose and the belly seam and repair each with a single domino. I kept my own hands off the line otherwise, to avoid bumping others' work.

Collaboration: I backed the fish idea early and said who was on which stretch. I asked Tom to hold off while I fixed the nose so we wouldn't bump, and I steered Priya onto the tail end of the bottom line so Maya and she could meet in the middle. I stayed clear of other people's stretches and called hands-off near the end so nothing got disturbed before the push.

Leadership: I helped set the plan: one push from the tail, round the nose, and back along the belly. I kept the team's work sequenced around the joins, which are the riskiest points, and gave clear calls as time got short, including the 5-minute reallocation of the bottom line and the final hands-off. Others did much of the building, and my contribution was mainly coordinating and verifying that the run was connected. I believe that was a meaningful part of why the fish held together, though it was a team result.", "my_share_percent": 30}
